transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess I came in because I just feel… wound up, almost all day. It’s hard to explain exactly, but it’s like my body is constantly bracing for something, even when nothing is actually happening. I’ll be sitting at my computer trying to work, and I can feel this tension in me, like I’m ready for some problem to pop up, even if I’m just doing ordinary things.

And then after dinner, when I should be relaxing, it doesn’t really switch off. I’ll sit down and think, “Okay, now I can calm down,” but my body still feels tight and on edge. It’s not dramatic every minute, but it’s there enough that I thought I should talk to someone about it.
Have you been experiencing any feelings of fear or worry that you can't control?

Yes… I think that’s exactly what’s been bothering me. It’s not like one huge fear all the time, it’s more that once a worry starts, I can’t seem to put it down. I’ll tell myself, “Daniela, enough, just focus on this report,” because I work at the computer and I need to stay on task, but then one small thought turns into five more.

Like I’ll think, “Did I miss a message?” and then I’m checking things, and then I’m replaying what could go wrong, or whether I should have responded differently, or what if something gets overlooked. And before I realize it, half an hour has gone by and I haven’t really done what I meant to do. It feels silly sometimes because I know I’m trying to reason with myself, but the worry doesn’t listen very well.
Do you ever have sudden, intense episodes of fear or discomfort that reach a peak within minutes?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, no. I mean, I do feel uncomfortable and tense, but it doesn’t usually come on suddenly like an attack or something that peaks really fast. It’s more… drawn out, if that makes sense. Like a steady buildup or background hum rather than this sharp wave that takes over in a few minutes.

Sometimes I’ll notice I’m very keyed up, but when I think back, it’s usually because I’ve been worrying for a while already, not because it came out of nowhere all at once. So I don’t think I’ve had those sudden intense episodes you’re describing.
Do you have recurring thoughts that feel intrusive or unwanted?

I don’t know if I’d call them intrusive in the way people sometimes mean, like a strange thought popping in out of nowhere, but yes, I do get thoughts I don’t want that sort of barge in and then won’t leave me alone.

It’s usually worry thoughts. I’ll be trying to work on a report, and I’ll literally tell myself, “Daniela, enough, focus on this report,” because I know I need to get it done. But then one small thing starts it—like wondering if I missed a message, or if something could go wrong—and suddenly it turns into five other thoughts. Then I’m checking messages, rereading things, replaying what I said or what might happen, and before I know it, half an hour has gone by.

So yes, they feel unwanted, and I don’t feel like I can just shut them off when I want to.
Do you feel like these worry thoughts are irrational or unrealistic?

Some of them, yes. I mean, I can usually see afterward that I was jumping ahead too far, or preparing for problems that hadn’t even happened. But in the moment it feels like I’m just being responsible, if that makes sense.

My mind keeps moving from one thing to another. I’ll start with something small, like, “Did I miss something at the office?” and then it becomes, “What if someone is waiting on me?” or “What if I forgot a detail?” Then it shifts to my sister in Arecibo, wondering if she’s okay, or my husband driving home, or whether I’m keeping up with church commitments, or bills coming due. It’s like my brain makes a whole list, and I feel like I have to mentally prepare for each possible thing going wrong.

So, rationally, I know not all of that is realistic at the same time. But it still feels hard to dismiss, because there’s always some little piece of it that could be true.
Do you find it difficult to control your worry on most days?

Yes, I do. Not every single minute of the day, but on most days, once the worrying starts, it’s really hard for me to pull myself back from it.

Like at work, I’ll be trying to finish something simple, like a report, and I’ll tell myself, “Daniela, enough, focus on this report,” because I know I’m losing time. But then one small thought comes in, like maybe I missed an email or maybe there’s something I forgot to check, and then that turns into five more thoughts. Then I’m checking messages, rereading what I already read, thinking through what could go wrong, and before I realize it, half an hour is gone.

And the frustrating part is that I know I’m doing it. It’s not like I’m unaware. I can see myself getting pulled into it, but it still feels very hard to stop.
Is your worry usually about a specific area of your life, like work or relationships, or does it seem to spread across many different areas?

It spreads, definitely. I wish it stayed in one box, like just work, because then maybe I could handle it more neatly, but it doesn’t.

It can start with work, like thinking I may have missed something at the office or didn’t answer someone quickly enough, and then before I know it my mind jumps to my sister in Arecibo and whether she’s okay, then to my husband driving home, then to church commitments I said I would help with, then bills or something around the house. It’s like one concern opens the door to the next one.

And a lot of the time I’m not even dealing with an actual problem in front of me. I’m preparing in my head for things that haven’t happened yet—what if this goes wrong, what if I forgot that, what if someone needs me and I’m not ready. So no, it’s not just one area. It moves around.
Has your worry been interfering with your daily life or activities in a significant way?

Yes, it has, though I wouldn’t say everything is falling apart or anything like that. I’m still going to work, I’m still getting my reports done, I still show up for my family and for church when I’ve said I would. So from the outside, I think people might say I’m functioning fine.

But it takes me longer than it used to. A report that should be straightforward can take extra time because I keep going back and checking it again, or rereading an email before I send it, or making sure I didn’t miss some detail. And sometimes I know I’ve already checked something, but I’ll still feel like I need to look one more time, just to be sure.

And with people I care about, I’ve noticed I can sound short or impatient, especially when my mind is already full. I don’t mean to, but then I’ll hear my tone afterward and feel bad, and I’ve had to apologize. So yes, it interferes—not in a way where I’ve stopped doing my life, but it makes things heavier and slower, and it affects how I am with people.
Do you often feel restless or like you're on edge, even when there's no apparent reason for it?

Yes… that’s actually a big part of why I came in. I feel wound up almost all day, like my body is bracing for something, even when there isn’t anything obvious happening.

It can be something completely ordinary, like I’m just sitting at my computer, not in a meeting, not dealing with a crisis, just doing regular work, and I still feel like I’m sort of tightened up inside. Like I’m waiting for something to go wrong or like I need to be ready to respond, even if there’s no real reason at that moment.

And then after dinner, when I should be relaxing, it doesn’t always just turn off. I’ll sit down and think, okay, now I can rest, but my body doesn’t seem to get the message. I’m still tense, still on alert. It’s not dramatic, like I’m pacing the room all day, but there’s this constant wound-up feeling that’s hard to shake.
How much distress do you feel your worry and tension are causing you on a daily basis?

It’s distressing most days, but I’d describe it as… manageable, I guess, not completely overwhelming. I’m still doing the things I’m supposed to do. I get to work, I finish my reports, I show up for my family, and I still go to church and help when I said I would. So it’s not like I’ve stopped functioning.

But inside, it feels like everything takes more effort than it should. A report that used to be pretty routine can take me much longer because I keep going back over it, checking details, rereading what I wrote, making sure I didn’t miss anything. And I know some of that sounds responsible, but it doesn’t feel calm or productive—it feels like I can’t quite trust that it’s okay.

And then with my family, or people close to me, I notice it comes out in my tone sometimes. I’ll sound short or impatient, and then I feel terrible afterward because they didn’t deserve that. I’ve had to apologize more than once, and that bothers me.

So daily distress… I’d say it’s there in the background a lot. I can get through the day, but it makes the day heavier, slower, and I don’t feel like myself as much as I’d like to.
Do you feel like you've been worrying excessively for more than six months?

Yes. It’s definitely been more than six months. I’d say about thirteen months now, if I’m counting it honestly.

It really seemed to start when my sister in Arecibo began needing a lot more help from the family. At first I thought, well, of course I’m worried, that’s normal, families go through things. But it didn’t really settle down after the first few weeks or months. It just kept going, and then the worrying became sort of… part of my daily rhythm, if that makes sense.

So yes, it’s been over a year now—around thirteen months.
Is your worry usually centered around one main issue, such as your sister's situation, or does it cover a wide range of topics and concerns?

It started with my sister, so at first I would have said it was mostly centered on her situation in Arecibo. That was the thing I could point to and say, “This is why I’m worried.”

But honestly, now it jumps around. It’s like my mind doesn’t stay on one track. I’ll be thinking about my sister and whether she needs something, and then suddenly I’m thinking about work—like, did I miss something in a report, did I send the wrong version, should I double-check that email again. Then it might shift to my husband driving home, and I’ll start imagining, what if something happens on the road, what if he doesn’t call when he said he would.

And then there are smaller things too, like church commitments, whether I promised to help with something and forgot a detail, or bills and whether I overlooked a payment. It’s not always one big crisis. Sometimes it’s just this chain of “what ifs,” one after another.

I find myself preparing for problems that haven’t even happened yet—like mentally rehearsing what I would do if something went wrong. So no, it’s not just my sister anymore. She’s still part of it, definitely, but the worry spreads into a lot of different areas.
Do you often notice that your worry is accompanied by physical sensations like muscle tension or tightness?

Yes, I do. That’s actually a big part of why I came in. I feel wound up almost all day, like my body is bracing for something, even when there isn’t anything happening right then.

It can be when I’m just sitting at my computer, doing something ordinary, and I’ll notice I’m holding myself really tight—like my shoulders or my whole posture is just… guarded. And then after dinner, when I should be relaxing, it’s still there. I’ll be sitting down, trying to unwind, and my body doesn’t seem to get the message that everything is okay.

It’s not always dramatic, but it’s persistent. Like I’m physically on alert most of the day.
Have you noticed any significant problems in your relationships or at work due to your worrying?

Yes… not in a dramatic way, like I haven’t lost my job or stopped talking to people or anything like that. I’m still functioning, I guess is the word. I show up to work, I get my reports done, I go to church, I’m there for my family.

But it does affect things. At work, reports take me longer than they used to because I’ll keep going back over them. I’ll check a number, then check it again, then wonder if I checked the right version, and before I know it I’ve spent way more time on something that should have been straightforward. I don’t think my work quality has fallen apart, but it takes more out of me, and it’s definitely slower.

With relationships, it’s more that I get tense and then I sound short. Like my husband or someone in the family will ask me something normal, and I’ll answer in this clipped tone because my mind is already full of five other worries. Then afterward I feel bad and I’ll have to apologize, because they didn’t deserve that. Same with people I care about at church sometimes—not that I’m yelling or anything, but I can come across impatient.

So… yes, there are problems, but I’d call them mild. I’m still doing what I need to do, but it feels harder, and I can tell it spills over onto other people sometimes.
Have you had to take days off work or significantly cut back on social activities because of your worrying?

Not really in the sense of taking full days off work, no. I’m still going in and getting things done. I haven’t cut out church or family things either — I still show up, and from the outside I probably look like I’m managing.

But it’s harder than it used to be. At work, I’ll finish a report, and then I’ll go back and check it again, and then I’ll start wondering if I checked the right version or missed something small. So things that should take a normal amount of time end up taking longer, and I feel more drained by them.

And socially or with family, I haven’t really stopped going, but I can tell the worry affects how I act. I’ll be tense and preoccupied, and then I’ll answer someone too sharply. I’ve had to apologize to my husband or people I care about because I sounded short when they hadn’t done anything wrong.

So I wouldn’t say I’ve significantly cut back, exactly. I’m still doing my responsibilities. It’s just… everything takes more effort, and sometimes it spills over into how I treat people.
Have you noticed that your worry is interfering with your ability to enjoy time with family and friends or perform your job to the best of your ability?

Yes, I think it does, although I’d still say I’m functioning. I don’t want to make it sound like everything has fallen apart, because it hasn’t. I’m still getting my work done, and I’m still showing up for my family and for church and doing the things I’m supposed to do.

But at work, it definitely affects how well I’m able to do things, or maybe how efficiently. Reports take me longer than they should because I keep double-checking them. I’ll finish something and then go back through it again, and then I’ll start second-guessing whether I checked the right thing or missed some small detail. So I do get it done, but it takes more time and more energy than it used to.

And with family and friends, yes, it gets in the way of enjoying the time sometimes. I’ll be there physically, but my mind is still caught up in whatever I’m worrying about, and then I can come across short or impatient. I’ve had to apologize to people I care about because I sounded clipped when they really hadn’t done anything wrong. That bothers me, because I don’t want them to feel like they’re the problem.
Would you say that your worrying is causing you significant distress or is getting in the way of your daily life in a major way?

I’d say it causes me distress, yes… but I’m not sure I’d call it “major” in the sense of my daily life stopping or me not being able to do things. I’m still getting my work done. I still go in, I still finish my reports, I’m still showing up for my family and for church. So from the outside, I think people would probably say I’m managing.

But it does get in the way. The work part is a good example — reports just take me longer than they used to because I keep going back and checking things. I’ll check something once, then I’ll think, “Did I check the right version?” or “What if I missed a small mistake?” and then I’m back in it again. So I’m doing the work, but it feels like it takes more effort than it should.

And with people close to me, it bothers me that I can sound short or impatient when I don’t mean to. I’ve had to apologize to my husband or family, or people I care about, because I answered in a clipped way when they hadn’t done anything wrong. That part makes me feel bad afterward.

So… significant distress, yes. Major interference, maybe not. I’m still functioning, but it’s definitely wearing on me and affecting my day-to-day more than I’d like.
Would you say that your worry is making it very hard for you to do your job or get along with others?

Very hard… I don’t know if I’d put it quite that strongly. I mean, I am still doing my job. I’m not missing deadlines in some obvious way, and I’m not avoiding people or staying home from church or family things. I still show up, and I still get things done.

But it does make things harder than they need to be. With work, especially reports, I’ll finish one and then keep going back over it. I’ll check it, then wonder if I checked the right part or the right version, or if there’s some small mistake I missed. So something that should be done just keeps stretching out, and by the end I feel worn out from all the extra checking.

And with people… I wouldn’t say I can’t get along with them, because I do care about them and I’m not trying to be difficult. But I can get tense and distracted, and then I’ll answer too sharply. I’ve had to go back and apologize to my husband or people I care about because I sounded short when they really didn’t deserve that.

So, not “very hard” like I can’t function, but yes, it definitely gets in the way and makes both work and relationships feel more strained than they should.
Have you ever experienced a sudden, intense fear or discomfort that peaked within minutes, which may have included symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or shortness of breath?

I’m not sure I’ve had something like that in the way you mean. I mean, I do get anxious, and I can feel worked up at times, but I don’t know that I’ve had a sudden episode where it just came out of nowhere and peaked within a few minutes like that.

When I worry, it usually feels more like it builds and stays with me, if that makes sense, rather than hitting all at once. I might be tense or preoccupied, but I can’t really point to a specific attack with a racing heart or sweating or shortness of breath. At least not that I’ve noticed or thought of that way.

And then after dinner, when I should be relaxing, it doesn’t always just turn off. I’ll sit down and think, okay, now I can rest, but my body doesn’t seem to get the message. I’m still tense, still on alert. It’s not dramatic, like I’m pacing the room all day, but there’s this constant wound-up feeling that’s hard to shake.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress
doctor.question: How much distress do you feel your worry and tension are causing you on a daily basis?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still getting my work done and showing up for family and church, but it takes me longer to finish reports, I double-check things more than I used to, and I’ve had to apologize for sounding short with people I care about.
target_item.reason: The question asks how much the worry and tension affect daily life through distress, which is most directly covered by the functional impairment profile describing how symptoms make work, relationships, and responsibilities harder.

patient.answer:
It’s distressing most days, but I’d describe it as… manageable, I guess, not completely overwhelming. I’m still doing the things I’m supposed to do. I get to work, I finish my reports, I show up for my family, and I still go to church and help when I said I would. So it’s not like I’ve stopped functioning.

But inside, it feels like everything takes more effort than it should. A report that used to be pretty routine can take me much longer because I keep going back over it, checking details, rereading what I wrote, making sure I didn’t miss anything. And I know some of that sounds responsible, but it doesn’t feel calm or productive—it feels like I can’t quite trust that it’s okay.

And then with my family, or people close to me, I notice it comes out in my tone sometimes. I’ll sound short or impatient, and then I feel terrible afterward because they didn’t deserve that. I’ve had to apologize more than once, and that bothers me.

So daily distress… I’d say it’s there in the background a lot. I can get through the day, but it makes the day heavier, slower, and I don’t feel like myself as much as I’d like to.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are persistent and uncontrollable enough to indicate generalized anxiety disorder
doctor.question: Do you feel like you've been worrying excessively for more than six months?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about thirteen months, since my sister in Arecibo started needing much more help from the family.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the excessive worry has persisted for more than six months, which is directly about the duration of symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yes. It’s definitely been more than six months. I’d say about thirteen months now, if I’m counting it honestly.

It really seemed to start when my sister in Arecibo began needing a lot more help from the family. At first I thought, well, of course I’m worried, that’s normal, families go through things. But it didn’t really settle down after the first few weeks or months. It just kept going, and then the worrying became sort of… part of my daily rhythm, if that makes sense.

So yes, it’s been over a year now—around thirteen months.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's excessive worry is focused on a specific issue or is more generalized
doctor.question: Is your worry usually centered around one main issue, such as your sister's situation, or does it cover a wide range of topics and concerns?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My mind keeps going from one concern to another—my sister in Arecibo, whether I missed something at the office, my husband driving home, church commitments, bills—and I find myself preparing for problems that haven’t even happened.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worry is focused on one issue or spans multiple topics, which directly matches excessive anxiety and worry about a number of events or activities.

patient.answer:
It started with my sister, so at first I would have said it was mostly centered on her situation in Arecibo. That was the thing I could point to and say, “This is why I’m worried.”

But honestly, now it jumps around. It’s like my mind doesn’t stay on one track. I’ll be thinking about my sister and whether she needs something, and then suddenly I’m thinking about work—like, did I miss something in a report, did I send the wrong version, should I double-check that email again. Then it might shift to my husband driving home, and I’ll start imagining, what if something happens on the road, what if he doesn’t call when he said he would.

And then there are smaller things too, like church commitments, whether I promised to help with something and forgot a detail, or bills and whether I overlooked a payment. It’s not always one big crisis. Sometimes it’s just this chain of “what ifs,” one after another.

I find myself preparing for problems that haven’t even happened yet—like mentally rehearsing what I would do if something went wrong. So no, it’s not just my sister anymore. She’s still part of it, definitely, but the worry spreads into a lot of different areas.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's worry is associated with muscle tension
doctor.question: Do you often notice that your worry is accompanied by physical sensations like muscle tension or tightness?

target_item.name: Restlessness_Tension
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I feel wound up almost all day, like my body is bracing for something, even when I’m just sitting at my computer or trying to relax after dinner.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical tension or tightness accompanying worry, which most directly matches feeling keyed up, on edge, and physically tense.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do. That’s actually a big part of why I came in. I feel wound up almost all day, like my body is bracing for something, even when there isn’t anything happening right then.

It can be when I’m just sitting at my computer, doing something ordinary, and I’ll notice I’m holding myself really tight—like my shoulders or my whole posture is just… guarded. And then after dinner, when I should be relaxing, it’s still there. I’ll be sitting down, trying to unwind, and my body doesn’t seem to get the message that everything is okay.

It’s not always dramatic, but it’s persistent. Like I’m physically on alert most of the day.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's worry is causing significant impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant problems in your relationships or at work due to your worrying?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still getting my work done and showing up for family and church, but it takes me longer to finish reports, I double-check things more than I used to, and I’ve had to apologize for sounding short with people I care about.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worrying has caused problems in work or relationships, which directly relates to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… not in a dramatic way, like I haven’t lost my job or stopped talking to people or anything like that. I’m still functioning, I guess is the word. I show up to work, I get my reports done, I go to church, I’m there for my family.

But it does affect things. At work, reports take me longer than they used to because I’ll keep going back over them. I’ll check a number, then check it again, then wonder if I checked the right version, and before I know it I’ve spent way more time on something that should have been straightforward. I don’t think my work quality has fallen apart, but it takes more out of me, and it’s definitely slower.

With relationships, it’s more that I get tense and then I sound short. Like my husband or someone in the family will ask me something normal, and I’ll answer in this clipped tone because my mind is already full of five other worries. Then afterward I feel bad and I’ll have to apologize, because they didn’t deserve that. Same with people I care about at church sometimes—not that I’m yelling or anything, but I can come across impatient.

So… yes, there are problems, but I’d call them mild. I’m still doing what I need to do, but it feels harder, and I can tell it spills over onto other people sometimes.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worry is causing significant impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Have you had to take days off work or significantly cut back on social activities because of your worrying?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still getting my work done and showing up for family and church, but it takes me longer to finish reports, I double-check things more than I used to, and I’ve had to apologize for sounding short with people I care about.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether the worrying has caused significant reductions in work attendance or social activities, which is directly about functional impact.

patient.answer:
Not really in the sense of taking full days off work, no. I’m still going in and getting things done. I haven’t cut out church or family things either — I still show up, and from the outside I probably look like I’m managing.

But it’s harder than it used to be. At work, I’ll finish a report, and then I’ll go back and check it again, and then I’ll start wondering if I checked the right version or missed something small. So things that should take a normal amount of time end up taking longer, and I feel more drained by them.

And socially or with family, I haven’t really stopped going, but I can tell the worry affects how I act. I’ll be tense and preoccupied, and then I’ll answer someone too sharply. I’ve had to apologize to my husband or people I care about because I sounded short when they hadn’t done anything wrong.

So I wouldn’t say I’ve significantly cut back, exactly. I’m still doing my responsibilities. It’s just… everything takes more effort, and sometimes it spills over into how I treat people.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worry is causing significant impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Have you noticed that your worry is interfering with your ability to enjoy time with family and friends or perform your job to the best of your ability?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still getting my work done and showing up for family and church, but it takes me longer to finish reports, I double-check things more than I used to, and I’ve had to apologize for sounding short with people I care about.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worry interferes with enjoyment of relationships and job performance, which directly concerns functional impairment in work, family, and social life.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think it does, although I’d still say I’m functioning. I don’t want to make it sound like everything has fallen apart, because it hasn’t. I’m still getting my work done, and I’m still showing up for my family and for church and doing the things I’m supposed to do.

But at work, it definitely affects how well I’m able to do things, or maybe how efficiently. Reports take me longer than they should because I keep double-checking them. I’ll finish something and then go back through it again, and then I’ll start second-guessing whether I checked the right thing or missed some small detail. So I do get it done, but it takes more time and more energy than it used to.

And with family and friends, yes, it gets in the way of enjoying the time sometimes. I’ll be there physically, but my mind is still caught up in whatever I’m worrying about, and then I can come across short or impatient. I’ve had to apologize to people I care about because I sounded clipped when they really hadn’t done anything wrong. That bothers me, because I don’t want them to feel like they’re the problem.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worry is causing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life
doctor.question: Would you say that your worrying is causing you significant distress or is getting in the way of your daily life in a major way?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still getting my work done and showing up for family and church, but it takes me longer to finish reports, I double-check things more than I used to, and I’ve had to apologize for sounding short with people I care about.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worry causes significant distress or interferes with daily life, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I’d say it causes me distress, yes… but I’m not sure I’d call it “major” in the sense of my daily life stopping or me not being able to do things. I’m still getting my work done. I still go in, I still finish my reports, I’m still showing up for my family and for church. So from the outside, I think people would probably say I’m managing.

But it does get in the way. The work part is a good example — reports just take me longer than they used to because I keep going back and checking things. I’ll check something once, then I’ll think, “Did I check the right version?” or “What if I missed a small mistake?” and then I’m back in it again. So I’m doing the work, but it feels like it takes more effort than it should.

And with people close to me, it bothers me that I can sound short or impatient when I don’t mean to. I’ve had to apologize to my husband or family, or people I care about, because I answered in a clipped way when they hadn’t done anything wrong. That part makes me feel bad afterward.

So… significant distress, yes. Major interference, maybe not. I’m still functioning, but it’s definitely wearing on me and affecting my day-to-day more than I’d like.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worry is causing significant impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Would you say that your worry is making it very hard for you to do your job or get along with others?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still getting my work done and showing up for family and church, but it takes me longer to finish reports, I double-check things more than I used to, and I’ve had to apologize for sounding short with people I care about.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worry is interfering with work performance and relationships with others, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Very hard… I don’t know if I’d put it quite that strongly. I mean, I am still doing my job. I’m not missing deadlines in some obvious way, and I’m not avoiding people or staying home from church or family things. I still show up, and I still get things done.

But it does make things harder than they need to be. With work, especially reports, I’ll finish one and then keep going back over it. I’ll check it, then wonder if I checked the right part or the right version, or if there’s some small mistake I missed. So something that should be done just keeps stretching out, and by the end I feel worn out from all the extra checking.

And with people… I wouldn’t say I can’t get along with them, because I do care about them and I’m not trying to be difficult. But I can get tense and distracted, and then I’ll answer too sharply. I’ve had to go back and apologize to my husband or people I care about because I sounded short when they really didn’t deserve that.

So, not “very hard” like I can’t function, but yes, it definitely gets in the way and makes both work and relationships feel more strained than they should.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of panic attacks
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced a sudden, intense fear or discomfort that peaked within minutes, which may have included symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or shortness of breath?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about sudden panic-like episodes peaking within minutes with physical symptoms, and the provided symptom profile does not include panic attacks or discrete episodes of intense fear.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’ve had something like that in the way you mean. I mean, I do get anxious, and I can feel worked up at times, but I don’t know that I’ve had a sudden episode where it just came out of nowhere and peaked within a few minutes like that.

When I worry, it usually feels more like it builds and stays with me, if that makes sense, rather than hitting all at once. I might be tense or preoccupied, but I can’t really point to a specific attack with a racing heart or sweating or shortness of breath. At least not that I’ve noticed or thought of that way.
